draft_note: Adapted from the preserved pitch structure and investor deck, using the owner's family-biographer direction. These are editable working drafts, not approved company facts. Confirm product availability, demonstrations, traction, pricing and the ask before pitching. No numerical traction, market or financial claims are assumed. Timing includes only the saved text at 130 words/minute; demonstrations and pauses need rehearsal.

pitches.title: The everyday introduction
pitches.body: A Story is an AI biographer for families. Think of the questions you still want to ask your parents or grandparents, but never find the right moment for. We're building a way to turn ordinary phone conversations into an ongoing family story, with an interviewer that remembers earlier conversations and asks useful follow-ups. The goal is simple: make it easier to ask, and give the family somewhere to keep the answer.

pitches.title: The investor introduction
pitches.body: We're building A Story, an ongoing AI biographer for families. Our initial customer hypothesis is an adult child who wants to preserve a willing parent's stories without becoming the interviewer and archivist. The product connects guided conversations with family context, so each interview can build on the last. Our next proof points are paid demand, repeat interviews and the actual cost of serving a family. I'd like to show you the experience and hear how you would test that thesis.

pitches.title: Explain it to a family
pitches.body: You probably have a photograph at home that raises a question. Who was there? What happened that day? Why did it matter? The person who knows may still be a phone call away, but arranging an interview and keeping track of everything can turn into a project that never happens. A Story is an AI biographer for families. We're building it around familiar conversations, with an interviewer that can remember what was discussed before and return to the details that deserve another question. The family can help supply context, and the story can grow over time instead of depending on one perfect interview. The simplest starting point is a willing parent or grandparent and the questions you want to ask them. What is one story you would want your family to understand better?

pitches.title: Invite a parent or grandparent
pitches.body: Your family may know what happened in your life without knowing how it felt to live it. They might recognize a place in a photograph but never have heard why you went there, who helped you, or what you learned. A Story is being built to help those conversations happen in a familiar way: by talking, starting with the stories you want to tell. Our aim is a guided interviewer that remembers earlier conversations, so you do not have to begin from the beginning every time. This should feel like an invitation, not a test or a performance. Before any interview, we would explain how it works and how your story will be used. Is there a moment you would enjoy telling your family about, in your own words?

pitches.title: Open a community partnership conversation
pitches.body: A Story is an AI biographer for families, built around a problem your community may recognize: people want to preserve personal stories, but somebody has to initiate the conversations, ask the follow-ups and organize the answers. We're exploring a familiar starting point, guided phone interviews with a willing storyteller, and a family archive that can grow as relatives contribute context. We would like to learn whether this approach is useful to the families you serve. A partnership would start with a small, clearly scoped pilot, with consent, responsibilities and success measures agreed in advance. We are not assuming you will distribute the product or that a partnership already exists. Could we discuss the needs you hear from families and what a responsible pilot would have to prove?

pitches.title: Explain the voice use case to a grant partner
pitches.body: A Story is an ongoing AI biographer for families. The voice problem is not just converting speech to text. A useful interviewer has to listen naturally, remember prior context and ask a follow-up that helps someone tell a richer story. Phone conversations are our simplest core experience; a visual interviewer is a possible extension for web and mobile. We want to evaluate voice tools against the actual interview task, including response speed, transcription quality, expressive conversation and cost per completed interview. Startup credits could support a focused comparison without forcing us to commit to a provider before we understand the trade-offs. We would define the experiment, show what is already working and clearly separate that from planned capabilities. Could your program support that kind of product evaluation?

pitches.title: Three-minute competition pitch
pitches.body:
A family photograph can outlive the story behind it. We know who is in the picture, but not always what happened before it, why somebody made a difficult choice, or what that moment meant to them. Often the answer is still available. The hard part is making time to ask, following the thread and preserving what we learn.

A Story is an ongoing AI biographer for families. We're building a simpler way to begin with familiar phone conversations, supported by an interviewer that remembers earlier conversations and family context. The goal is not one perfect recording. It is a story that can grow over time.

Our initial customer hypothesis is an adult child who wants to give a willing parent or grandparent the chance to tell their story, without becoming the interviewer, editor and archivist. That distinction matters. The storyteller needs an experience that feels comfortable. The family organizer needs the process to be manageable. We need to prove that both see enough value to keep using it.

Imagine a storyteller describing an old photograph. A relative adds a name or recalls the event differently. A later interview can ask about that contribution. This is an illustrative example of the family loop we want to test, not a claim about an observed customer result. The question is whether shared context leads to better conversations and a more useful archive.

[Add one sentence about the current product and a genuine proof point, or describe the next validation test.]

Other products already help families capture memories. We will not claim that phone interviews or archives are unique. Our bet is that continuity between conversations, with family contributions informing the next question, can reduce the work of preserving a family history. That has to be demonstrated.

Our next milestones are clear: understand paid demand, help storytellers complete the first and second interviews, and measure the actual cost and support required per family. Support from this program would be tied to those tests rather than an unsupported growth forecast.

[Insert the exact program-specific request and what it enables.]

A Story makes the conversation easier to begin and gives the family somewhere to keep the answer. There is still time to ask.

pitches.title: Three-minute application video
pitches.body:
[Introduce the eligible presenter by name and role. Confirm this program's current rules for video, slides and demonstrations.]

Think of one question you still want to ask somebody in your family. It might be about the place they grew up, a person in an old photograph, or a choice that changed the direction of their life. The answer may still be there, but recording a useful family story takes more than asking once. Somebody has to arrange the conversation, follow up on the details and keep the answers accessible.

A Story is an ongoing AI biographer for families. Our simplest core experience is a familiar phone conversation with a guided interviewer. We're building continuity into that experience, so the interviewer can remember earlier conversations and family context rather than treating every call as a new introduction.

The initial customer hypothesis is an adult child buying for a willing parent or grandparent. We want to make the organizer's job easier while giving the storyteller a reason to participate again. A family member might contribute context about a photograph, a name or an event. That contribution could become a thoughtful question in a later interview. This is the family loop we want to validate.

[Describe a current, demonstrated capability. If it is only a planned behavior, say so plainly.]

We know there are established ways to capture family memories. Our proposed advantage is not simply that we use AI or offer phone calls. It is the connection between family input, remembered context and the next useful conversation. The value of that connection has to be proven with real families.

The business questions are equally practical. Will the intended buyer pay? Will the storyteller return for another call? What does a completed interview cost, including voice tools and support? These are the milestones we intend to measure before making large growth claims.

[Add a verified team capability relevant to delivering this plan.]

[Close with the program-specific request and the evidence it will help produce.]

We want fewer family stories to stay behind a question that nobody found time to ask. A Story gives the family a way to begin that conversation and keep building on it.

pitches.title: Five-minute investor conversation
pitches.body:
We inherit the photograph, but not always the context. A Story starts with that familiar problem: families want to know more about one another, yet collecting a useful history becomes a job somebody has to take on. The organizer schedules interviews, comes up with questions, follows the story and keeps the results. Good intentions alone do not make that happen.

A Story is an ongoing AI biographer for families. We're building around familiar phone conversations, with an interviewer that remembers earlier context and asks useful follow-ups. The family should be able to add a detail and see it become part of a later conversation. The archive is the result; the recurring interview experience is what creates it.

Our first buyer hypothesis is an adult child who wants to give a willing parent or grandparent a way to share their story. We are treating willingness to pay and repeat participation as separate things to prove. A gift can be purchased once and still fail as a product if the storyteller never takes another call.

Here is the experience we are working toward. A parent describes a photograph. A relative adds a name or remembers another side of the event. The next conversation can explore that addition, with the storyteller's perspective kept distinct from the relative's. This example explains the product thesis; it is not a real transcript or an observed outcome.

[Demonstrate the current experience. Label mockups and scripted examples. Allow about 45 seconds for a permitted demonstration.]

There are strong alternatives for collecting memories, including products with guided calls and shared archives. Our bet is that family contributions improving subsequent interviews can create a more useful ongoing experience. We should compare that on the actual user task, not claim uniqueness from an AI label.

[Add evidence from a real customer conversation, paid pilot or repeat interview. If none is available, state the current stage and the next test.]

The commercial model needs to be tested against real usage. Voice costs, hosting, support and fulfillment all matter. We are not presenting historical deck prices as current pricing, or a cost model as an observed margin. The first economics work should connect a defined offer to actual interview minutes and support load in the same cohort.

For distribution, we would start with one buyer segment, one purchase moment and one channel. The funnel would measure a paid gift, a completed first interview and a second interview. Partnerships and referrals are options to test, not existing arrangements we can claim.

A Story Technologies, Inc. is bootstrapped. The next financing discussion should be about which evidence a defined amount of capital or program support would unlock.

[Insert current team capabilities, the intended milestone, the exact ask and the period it funds. Do not imply that a financing amount has already been agreed.]

What we want to learn is whether an adult child's intention becomes a repeat experience that the storyteller values and the business can afford to deliver. If that works, there is a reason to expand. If it does not, we will know which part of the offer to change.

I'd like to discuss the assumptions you would challenge first and what evidence you would need before a next conversation. There is still time to ask the questions behind the photograph. A Story is being built to make that easier.

pitches.title: Seven-minute product demonstration
pitches.body:
WORKING OUTLINE - a seven-minute slot, including the demonstration. The text below is not seven minutes of finished speech.

Opening - 45 seconds
A Story is an ongoing AI biographer for families. Start with a familiar question behind a family photograph. Explain who the organizer and willing storyteller are.
[Use a real family example with permission, or label an example illustrative.]

The conversation - 2 minutes
Show the currently working interview experience. Keep the phone conversation as the simplest starting point. Explain what the interviewer knows and how a follow-up is chosen.
[Insert the exact current product flow. Clearly label planned features and mockups.]

The family loop - 90 seconds
Show one family contribution and how it could inform a later question. Distinguish the storyteller's words from a relative's contribution.
[Use permissioned customer material or label a scripted demonstration.]

The archive - 1 minute
Show how a family would find an earlier story and add context. Explain only the privacy, sharing and control behaviors that have been confirmed.
[Verify these controls before demonstrating them.]

Questions and next step - 105 seconds
Ask what felt useful and what felt uncomfortable. Explain the current availability and the next step without promising an unverified launch date or price.
[Insert the confirmed next step for this audience.]

pitches.title: Ten-minute technical partner briefing
pitches.body:
WORKING OUTLINE - ten minutes including questions and a product demonstration.

1. Product and user task - 90 seconds
A Story is an ongoing AI biographer for families. Explain why natural conversation, continuity and useful follow-ups matter more than a one-off voice interaction. Identify the organizer and willing storyteller.

2. Current implementation - 2 minutes
[Describe the actual current stack, integrations and product capabilities. Do not use an explored provider as a production integration.]
Show the simplest phone interview flow.

3. A concrete conversation - 2 minutes
[Demonstrate a permissioned interview or a clearly labeled scripted example.]
Show where prior conversation and family context affect the next question. Separate current behavior from planned functionality.

4. Proposed partner experiment - 2 minutes
Compare response speed, transcription quality, voice expressiveness and cost per completed interview. Explain the intended workload and integration effort.
[Insert the confirmed provider use case and success criteria.]

5. Optional visual interviewer - 90 seconds
Explain the proposed web/mobile avatar extension while keeping phone calls as the core experience. Personalization may include purpose, appearance, personality, voice and knowledge. The interview and memory system controls context.
[Label avatar capability as an exploration unless demonstrated.]

6. Request and next step - 1 minute
[State a specific credit, technical-support or evaluation request. Review publicity, renewal, overage and data terms before accepting anything.]
Close with the experiment the support would enable and the evidence we would share.

pitches.title: Fifteen-minute competition finals
pitches.body:
WORKING OUTLINE - adapted from the preserved 14-slide pitch structure. This is a fifteen-minute delivery plan, not a finished fifteen-minute script. Confirm the current program's rules separately.

A Story - 30 seconds
A Story is an ongoing AI biographer for families, built around familiar conversations and a family story that grows over time.

The unanswered question - 75 seconds
[Introduce one authentic family moment or a permissioned photograph.]
Reveal the detail that only the person who lived it can explain. Avoid invented personal stories.

The work families postpone - 75 seconds
Explain the organizer's job: initiating interviews, following up, keeping the answers and involving relatives.
[Add one verified, relevant research finding only if it improves the argument. Do not treat interest in family history as willingness to pay.]

First buyer and why now - 45 seconds
Present the adult-child buyer and willing-storyteller hypothesis. Explain why a familiar phone conversation is the starting point, not proof that every older adult wants an AI call.

The offer - 60 seconds
A gift becomes a sequence of conversations and a shared record the family can enrich. Show who does what.
[Confirm actual product availability and the current offer.]

One interview - 90 seconds
[Play permissioned audio or demonstrate the current product. Label a scripted example or mockup.]
Show a substantive follow-up. Explain only capabilities that are actually present.

The family loop - 60 seconds
Show a photograph, a contribution from a relative and the next useful question. Separate observed behavior from the proposed loop.

What exists and what we learned - 75 seconds
[Show genuine product status, completed interviews, payments or customer feedback, with dates and sources. If unavailable, describe the next validation test.]

Alternatives and our bet - 60 seconds
Compare the nearest alternatives fairly on guided calls, family input, attribution and continuity. The proposed advantage is family contributions improving later interviews. Its value needs proof.

Reachable opportunity - 60 seconds
[Explain the first buyer and accessible channel. Add a sourced bottom-up market argument only after review.]
Keep universal-adoption calculations and unsupported share forecasts out of the main story.

Business model - 75 seconds
[Insert current approved pricing and observed costs, or clearly labeled modeled costs.]
Explain interview usage, voice cost, support and fulfillment. A model is not an observed company margin.

First distribution experiment - 75 seconds
[Pick one channel and purchase moment.]
Measure paid gift conversion, first interview completion, second interview completion and cost in the same cohort. Do not claim a partnership that does not exist.

Next proof and the request - 90 seconds
[State the actual next milestone, team responsibilities, exact program-specific ask and what it enables.]
Tie support to evidence rather than an unsupported growth promise.

Close - 30 seconds
Return to the opening question. A Story makes the conversation easier to begin and gives the family somewhere to keep the answer.

pitches.title: Twenty-minute investor deep dive
pitches.body:
WORKING OUTLINE - a twenty-minute meeting presentation with demonstration and evidence discussion. Use the fifteen-minute core and spend the extra time on proof, not additional feature claims.

Opening and stakes - 2 minutes
A Story is an ongoing AI biographer for families. Begin with an authentic question behind a family photograph. Explain the work of organizing repeated conversations and preserving the answers.
[Choose a permissioned example. Do not invent a founder origin story.]

Buyer and product thesis - 2 minutes
Our first buyer hypothesis is an adult child buying for a willing parent or grandparent. Explain why the organizer and storyteller have different needs. The proposed family loop connects relatives' contributions to the next useful interview.
[State which behaviors currently exist and which are planned.]

Interview and archive demonstration - 4 minutes
[Show an actual current product flow or clearly labeled prototype.]
Demonstrate one useful follow-up, a family contribution and the archive. Explain consent, attribution and access only where confirmed. Leave room for a real conversation instead of narrating a feature list.

Evidence and unresolved questions - 3 minutes
[Present dated, source-linked evidence of interviews, paid demand, repeat use, customer feedback and actual costs. If unavailable, show the current stage and the tests required.]
Separate a waitlist, an interested customer and a paid repeat user. Keep fictional examples out of traction.

Alternatives and differentiation - 2 minutes
Compare the closest ways a family can do this job. Guided calls and shared archives already exist elsewhere. Explain the hypothesis that family context creates better subsequent interviews, and how you will measure whether it matters.
[Update competitor details before presenting.]

Business model and economics - 3 minutes
[Insert approved current pricing and a transparent cost model or observed cohort economics.]
Discuss actual minutes, voice costs, support, fees, hosting and any book fulfillment. Show sensitivity to usage and cost. Historical deck arithmetic does not establish realized margins or acquisition cost.

Acquisition and reachable market - 2 minutes
[Choose one initial buyer/channel combination and a measurable funnel.]
Explain the path from outreach to paid gift, first interview and second interview. Market context is not a forecast. Proposed partners are not contracted distribution.

Team, milestone and ask - 90 seconds
A Story Technologies, Inc. is bootstrapped.
[State current team capabilities, missing skills, the exact proposed financing or support request and the milestone it funds. Confirm the amount before using it.]
Define what would cause the team to expand, adjust the offer or stop an unsuccessful experiment.

Close - 30 seconds
There is still time to ask. Return to the opening photograph and invite discussion of the assumptions that need the strongest proof.
